claim: NF-κB plays key roles in inflammation and cancer.
source: NF-κB, which plays key roles in inflammation and cancer, displays oscillations whose biological advantage remains unclear.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation context and general scientific knowledge about NF-κB function.

claim: NF-κB displays oscillations whose biological advantage remains unclear.
source: NF-κB, which plays key roles in inflammation and cancer, displays oscillations whose biological advantage remains unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in understanding about the functional significance of NF-κB oscillations.

claim: Recent work indicated that NF-κB displays sustained oscillations that can be entrained.
source: Recent work indicated that NF-κB displays sustained oscillations that can be entrained, that is, reach a persistent synchronized state through small periodic perturbations.
evidence: This claim references prior published work on NF-κB dynamics.

claim: For GFP-p65 knock-in cells, NF-κB behaves as a damped oscillator able to synchronize to a variety of periodic external perturbations with no memory.
source: We show here that for our GFP-p65 knock-in cells NF-κB behaves as a damped oscillator able to synchronize to a variety of periodic external perturbations with no memory.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental observations and analysis.

claim: Transcription of NF-κB-controlled genes oscillates under synchronous NF-κB dynamics.
source: We imposed synchronous dynamics to prove that transcription of NF-κB-controlled genes also oscillates, but mature transcript levels follow three distinct patterns.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental manipulation and measurement of gene expression.

claim: Mature transcript levels of NF-κB-controlled genes follow three distinct patterns.
source: We imposed synchronous dynamics to prove that transcription of NF-κB-controlled genes also oscillates, but mature transcript levels follow three distinct patterns.
evidence: This is a key finding from genome-wide expression profiling experiments.

claim: Two sets of transcripts accumulate fast or slowly, respectively.
source: Two sets of transcripts accumulate fast or slowly, respectively.
evidence: This describes two of the three patterns observed in the transcriptional response.

claim: Chemokine and chemokine receptor mRNAs oscillate and reset at each new stimulus, with no memory of the past.
source: Another set, comprising chemokine and chemokine receptor mRNAs, oscillates and resets at each new stimulus, with no memory of the past.
evidence: This describes the third pattern of gene expression dynamics observed experimentally.

claim: TF oscillatory dynamics is a means of segmenting time to provide renewing opportunity windows for decision.
source: We propose that TF oscillatory dynamics is a means of segmenting time to provide renewing opportunity windows for decision.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the biological significance of the observed dynamics.

claim: Oscillatory dynamics with periods far shorter than 24 hr have been reported in genetic circuits of bacteria, yeast and mammalian cells.
source: However, oscillatory dynamics with periods far shorter than 24 hr have been reported in genetic circuits of bacteria (Suel et al., 2007), yeast (Cai et al., 2008; Hao and O'Shea, 2012) and mammalian cells (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2006; Hoffmann et al., 2002; Larson et al., 2013; Nelson et al., 2004; Shankaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The dynamics of transcription factors in gene circuits can play a key role in information transmission through biochemical networks.
source: The dynamics of transcription factors in gene circuits can play a key role in information transmission through biochemical networks (Selimkhanov et al., 2014) by selectively modulating the expression of different genes (Purvis and Lahav, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on transcription factor dynamics.

claim: Different p53 dynamics can selectively activate transcriptional programs that commit the cell to different cell fate decisions.
source: A paradigmatic example is how different p53 dynamics can selectively activate transcriptional programs that commit the cell to different cell fate decisions (Purvis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an example from the literature cited to support the concept of dynamic encoding.

claim: Entrainment is a property of free oscillating systems by which an oscillator can gradually modulate its phase and frequency thanks to a small periodic perturbation.
source: A property of free oscillating systems (or free oscillators, as analogy to simple mechanical oscillators such as the pendulum) is entrainment, by which an oscillator can gradually modulate its phase and frequency thanks to a small perturbation (forcing) that is itself periodic and oscillating with a period resonant with the intrinsic period of the oscillator (Pikovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a definition from the physics literature on oscillatory systems.

claim: Entrainment was successfully reproduced in synthetic genetic oscillators in bacterial cells.
source: Entrainment was successfully reproduced in synthetic genetic oscillators, in which single bacterial cells (each expressing a fluorescent reporter protein in response to a synthetic genetic circuit) were entrained collectively to an oscillating provision of arabinose (Mondragon-Palomino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In resting cells, p65 exists mostly within a cytoplasmic complex bound to the IκB inhibitors.
source: In resting cells, p65 exists mostly within a cytoplasmic complex bound to the IκB inhibitors (Hoffmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB regulation, supported by citation.

claim: Inflammatory signals like TNF-α or LPS induce phosphorylation of IκB proteins by IKKs, ubiquitination and degradation of IκBs, and the release of active NF-κB that translocates into the nucleus.
source: Inflammatory signals like tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induce phosphorylation of IκB proteins by IKKs–upstream kinases in the signaling pathway–, ubiquitination and degradation of IκBs, and the release of active NF-κB that translocates into the nucleus to activate the expression of several genes, including those encoding for the IκB inhibitors (Hoffmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the canonical NF-κB activation pathway, supported by citation.

claim: Re-expression of IκBs contributes to relocate NF-κB in the cytoplasm, which is an inhibitory feedback loop for the system.
source: Re-expression of IκBs contributes to relocate NF-κB in the cytoplasm, which is an inhibitory feedback loop for the system.
evidence: This describes a key regulatory mechanism in the NF-κB system.

claim: A20 provides a second feedback loop by inhibiting the IKKs upon activation of the system.
source: A second feedback loop is centred on the protein A20 (Ashall et al., 2009), which upon activation of the system inhibits the IKKs.
evidence: This describes another regulatory mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: The two feedback loops provide a nonredundant regulation of NF-κB response to external stimuli.
source: Thus, these two layers provide a nonredundant regulation of NF-κB response to external stimuli (Werner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on NF-κB regulation.

claim: Upon constant stimulation the nuclear concentration of NF-κB in each cell oscillates with heterogeneous dynamics according to each cell's susceptibility and to the inherent stochasticity of the system.
source: As a consequence of this complex wiring, upon constant stimulation the nuclear concentration of NF-κB in each cell oscillates with heterogeneous dynamics according to each cell's susceptibility and to the inherent stochasticity of the system (Nelson et al., 2004; Tay et al., 2010; Zambrano et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior single-cell studies.

claim: Due to asynchrony at the single cell level, the NF-κB response appears almost non-oscillating at the cell population level.
source: Due to such asynchrony at the single cell level, the NF-κB response appears almost non-oscillating at the cell population level (Hoffmann et al., 2002), and it is difficult to correlate NF-κB oscillatory profiles with gene expression outputs.
evidence: This is an inference from single-cell heterogeneity, supported by citation.

claim: Short trains of TNF-α pulses produce rounds of synchronous NF-κB translocation.
source: White's group showed that short trains of TNF-α pulses produce rounds of synchronous NF-κB translocation; the stimulation frequency affected both the translocation amplitude and gene expression levels (Ashall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Entrainment of NF-κB oscillations at population level arises when 3T3 cells stably transfected with GFP-p65 are perturbed with regular trains of sawtooth-like profiles of TNF-α.
source: A study performed while the present one was in progress indicated that entrainment of NF-κB oscillations at population level arises when 3T3 cells stably transfected with GFP-p65 are perturbed with regular trains of sawtooth-like profiles of TNF-α (Kellogg and Tay, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a concurrent study.

claim: GFP-p65 MEFs lock their NF-κB oscillations to the periodic external signal and become synchronized.
source: We find that GFP-p65 MEFs lock their NF-κB oscillations to the periodic external signal, and become synchronized.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The 1:1 locking of NF-κB oscillations is maintained over a wide variety of frequencies of the driving TNF-α stimulus.
source: However, the 1:1 locking is maintained over a wide variety of frequencies of the driving TNF-α stimulus, does not improve over repeated stimulation and actually disappears fast when the external stimulus ceases, all of which suggest that entrainment is not achieved.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations across multiple forcing conditions.

claim: The synchronization does not improve over repeated stimulation.
source: However, the 1:1 locking is maintained over a wide variety of frequencies of the driving TNF-α stimulus, does not improve over repeated stimulation and actually disappears fast when the external stimulus ceases, all of which suggest that entrainment is not achieved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of synchrony intensity over successive forcing cycles.

claim: Synchronization disappears fast when the external stimulus ceases.
source: However, the 1:1 locking is maintained over a wide variety of frequencies of the driving TNF-α stimulus, does not improve over repeated stimulation and actually disappears fast when the external stimulus ceases, all of which suggest that entrainment is not achieved.
evidence: This is shown in experiments where forcing is stopped and synchrony is lost rapidly.

claim: The mathematical model suggests that NF-κB can behave as a damped oscillator.
source: The mathematical model we developed indeed suggests that NF-κB can behave as a damped oscillator, analogous to a mechanical damped harmonic oscillator; damped oscillators do not entrain but follow external forcing while it is present.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling and simulations.

claim: One single NF-κB dynamics translates into 3 different dynamics of transcriptional regulation.
source: We find that one single NF-κB dynamics translates into 3 different dynamics of transcriptional regulation, all of which can be reproduced by our mathematical model; the key discriminator is the parameter representing mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genome-wide expression profiling and clustering analysis.

claim: The key discriminator between different transcriptional dynamics patterns is the parameter representing mRNA degradation.
source: We find that one single NF-κB dynamics translates into 3 different dynamics of transcriptional regulation, all of which can be reproduced by our mathematical model; the key discriminator is the parameter representing mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is determined through mathematical modeling and parameter fitting.

claim: The three dynamical patterns correspond to specific functions.
source: Furthermore, the three dynamical patterns correspond to specific functions, which suggests that group of genes were positively selected by evolution.
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis showing functional coherence within clusters.

claim: Constant stimulation of GFP-p65 knock-in cells with 10 ng/ml TNF-α for up to 15 hr induced nuclear-to-cytoplasmic p65 oscillations.
source: Constant stimulation of GFP-p65 knock-in cells in the microfluidic plate with a constant flow of 10 ng/ml TNF-α for up to 15 hr induced nuclear-to-cytoplasmic p65 oscillations (Figure 1B; Video 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) that are qualitatively similar to the heterogeneous oscillations observed with static stimulation (Sung et al., 2009; Zambrano et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results.

claim: Cells under constant flow of fresh medium without TNF-α divide and show almost no cell death.
source: Cells under constant flow of fresh medium without TNF-α divide and show almost no cell death (Video 2); cell death observed under continuous flow depends on the dose of TNF-α (Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Video 1) independently of the imaging conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through control experiments and video documentation.

claim: UV-induced DNA damage due to imaging is negligible as assessed by immunostaining for thymine dimers.
source: UV-induced DNA damage due to imaging (Cadet et al., 2005) is negligible as assessed by immunostaining for thymine dimers (Komatsu et al., 1997; Sinha and Hader, 2002).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: DNA Damage Response is negligible as assessed by immunostaining of imaged cells for gammaH2AX.
source: DNA Damage Response (DDR) is also negligible as assessed by immunostaining of imaged cells for gammaH2AX (Marti et al., 2006; Oh et al., 2011; Staszewski et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining experiments.

claim: Neither Hoechst exposure nor TNF-α affect dramatically the cell cycle.
source: Moreover, neither Hoechst exposure nor TNF-α affect dramatically the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is shown through FACS analysis of cell cycle distribution.

claim: The timing between two consecutive peaks (Texp) has a distribution with a maximum at 90 min.
source: Texp has a distribution with a maximum at 90 min (Figure 1F), which is the approximate intrinsic period reported for NF-κB oscillations that we called T0 (Nelson et al., 2004; Tay et al., 2010; Zambrano et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The heterogeneous oscillations are damped and tend to converge to an equilibrium state under stimulation.
source: The tail in the period distribution (Figure 1F) and the observed average of four peaks in 12 hr of stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), instead of the expected eight, indicate that in our cells the heterogeneous oscillations are damped and tend to converge to an equilibrium state under stimulation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from quantitative analysis of peak frequency over time.

claim: A minimal deterministic model that takes into account the basic elements of the NF-κB genetic circuit shows that different combinations of the parameters can lead to different dynamics.
source: Indeed, a minimal deterministic model that takes into account the basic elements of the NF-κB genetic circuit (Zambrano et al., 2014b) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, see Materials and methods for a complete description of the model) shows that different combinations of the parameters can lead to different dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical modeling and parameter exploration.

claim: The vast majority of parameter combinations give rise to damped oscillations.
source: The vast majority of parameter combinations give rise to damped oscillations (when all the eigenvalues have all negative real parts, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown through systematic parameter exploration and stability analysis.

claim: A smaller fraction of parameter combinations give rise to trajectories that converge to a stable limit cycle around the unstable fixed points.
source: A smaller fraction of parameter combinations give rise to trajectories that converge to a stable limit cycle around the unstable fixed points (so certain eigenvalues have positive real parts, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown through mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: Parameters for oscillating and non-oscillating cells are in similar intervals suggesting that it is the precise combination of the parameters, rather than a single one, what determines the resulting dynamics.
source: Interestingly, parameters for oscillating and non-oscillating cells are in similar intervals suggesting that it is the precise combination of the parameters, rather than a single one, what determines the resulting dynamics (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from parameter sensitivity analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Single cells activate NF-κB signalling synchronously to external TNF-α stimulation.
source: Our results show that single cells activate NF-κB signalling synchronously to external TNF-α stimulation, and that repeated forcing elicits synchronous NF-κB oscillations at population level.
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging experiments with periodic forcing.

claim: Repeated forcing elicits synchronous NF-κB oscillations at population level.
source: Our results show that single cells activate NF-κB signalling synchronously to external TNF-α stimulation, and that repeated forcing elicits synchronous NF-κB oscillations at population level.
evidence: This is shown through phase plots and synchrony analysis.

claim: NF-κB does not behave as a free oscillator: no cell oscillates constantly in the presence of continuous stimulation.
source: However, NF-κB does not behave as a free oscillator: no cell oscillates constantly in the presence of continuous stimulation (Figure 8A and B left, green lines).
evidence: This is demonstrated through long-term imaging under constant stimulation.

claim: Cells can be synchronized with a wide variety of forcing periods and forcing amplitudes.
source: Finally, cells can be synchronized with a wide variety of forcing periods and forcing amplitudes, and synchronize to the external forcing (Figure 8A and B right, green lines) without showing any preference for periods resonating with the NF-κB intrinsic period of 90 min; synchronization is more pronounced with high than with low stimulation amplitude.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic variation of forcing parameters.

claim: Cells synchronize to the external forcing without showing any preference for periods resonating with the NF-κB intrinsic period of 90 min.
source: Finally, cells can be synchronized with a wide variety of forcing periods and forcing amplitudes, and synchronize to the external forcing (Figure 8A and B right, green lines) without showing any preference for periods resonating with the NF-κB intrinsic period of 90 min; synchronization is more pronounced with high than with low stimulation amplitude.
evidence: This is shown by successful synchronization at 45, 60, 90, and 180 min periods.

claim: Synchronization is more pronounced with high than with low stimulation amplitude.
source: Finally, cells can be synchronized with a wide variety of forcing periods and forcing amplitudes, and synchronize to the external forcing (Figure 8A and B right, green lines) without showing any preference for periods resonating with the NF-κB intrinsic period of 90 min; synchronization is more pronounced with high than with low stimulation amplitude.
evidence: This is shown through quantification of synchrony intensity at different TNF-α doses.

claim: The ability of NF-κB to oscillate in tune with a forcing of 45 min illustrates the plasticity of synchronization.
source: The ability of NF-κB to oscillate in tune with a forcing of 45 min illustrates well the plasticity of synchronization: 45 min is equivalent to one half of the intrinsic period, and entrained cells would skip one forcing period out of 2 (following the 1:2 resonance), but our data do not support this interpretation, since cells only infrequently skip a forcing period.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with 45 min forcing period.

claim: GFP-p65 knock-in cells are not entrained, as they do not satisfy the essential precondition of sustained oscillations.
source: Thus, we find that our GFP-p65 knock-in cells are not entrained, as do not satisfy the essential precondition – sustained oscillations – and two critical tests for entrainment – increasing synchronization upon repeated forcing, and synchronization to the natural frequency of the internal oscillator (Pikovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is concluded based on multiple lines of experimental evidence and comparison to entrainment criteria.

claim: GFP-p65 knock-in cells appear closer to a damped harmonic oscillator whose frequency corresponds to the frequency of the external stimulation.
source: Our cells appear closer to the classical textbook example of a damped harmonic oscillator (Goldstein et al., 2001), whose frequency corresponds to the frequency of the external stimulation, and whose synchronization to the external stimulus increase monotonically with stimulus amplitude.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed behavior and comparison to physical oscillator models.

claim: The damped oscillator behaviour of the NF-κB system allows it to adapt to a wide variety of inputs and to quickly reset.
source: We interpret the damped oscillator behaviour of the NF-κB system as an intrinsic characteristic of the NF-κB system which allows it to adapt to a wide variety of inputs and to quickly reset.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the functional significance of the observed dynamics.

claim: Pathogens and inflammatory signals do not come in regular periodic patterns.
source: In fact, pathogens and inflammatory signals do not come in regular periodic patterns, and a carefully calibrated inflammatory response that would adapt itself to any irregular pattern of stimulation would be positively selected for.
evidence: This is a biological reasoning about the evolutionary context of NF-κB signaling.

claim: Simulations suggest that sustained oscillations would not be the norm, but rather the result of a specific set of parameters.
source: Our simulations suggest that sustained oscillations would not be the norm, but rather the result of a specific set of parameters (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is based on systematic parameter exploration with the mathematical model.

claim: The NF-κB network has an equilibrium that depending on the combinations of parameters can be stable or unstable.
source: Indeed, the NF-κB network has an equilibrium that depending on the combinations of parameters can be stable, giving rise to damped oscillations that converge to it, or unstable, giving rise to a stable cycle around it (see e.g. Figure 8B, left, magenta line); transitions between these two states can be mediated by a Hopf bifurcation.
evidence: This is determined through mathematical stability analysis of the model.

claim: The oscillatory behaviour of NF-κB consists in periodic relocalization between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
source: The oscillatory behaviour of NF-κB consists in periodic relocalization between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, and entails corresponding cycles of NF-κB binding to cognate binding sites in the genome.
evidence: This is a description of the observed NF-κB dynamics.

claim: NF-κB driven transcription is pulsatile.
source: Thus, NF-κB driven transcription should be pulsatile as well, and in fact we detect cycles in the levels of elongating transcripts in the prototypical early and late NF-κB-controlled genes IkBα and Ccl5.
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR measurements of nascent transcripts.

claim: Mature mRNA oscillates for IκBα.
source: However, whereas mature mRNA oscillates for IκBα, it slowly accumulates for the late gene Ccl5, and this held true for different frequencies of the periodic stimulation.
evidence: This is shown through qPCR measurements of mature transcripts.

claim: Mature mRNA slowly accumulates for the late gene Ccl5.
source: However, whereas mature mRNA oscillates for IκBα, it slowly accumulates for the late gene Ccl5, and this held true for different frequencies of the periodic stimulation.
evidence: This is shown through qPCR measurements.

claim: Genes with increasing transcription are predicted NF-κB targets.
source: While the genes with increasing transcription are predicted NF-κB targets, those in the decreasing sets are not.
evidence: This is shown through enrichment analysis against known NF-κB target gene lists.

claim: Genes in Cluster 1 display a clear and sustained oscillation in transcript level.
source: The train of p65 nuclear translocations is thus decoded by the cell into different transcriptional dynamics: genes in Cluster 1 display a clear and sustained oscillation in transcript level; instead, transcripts for genes in Clusters 2 and 3 accumulate fast or increase slowly and steadily over many cycles of NF-κB oscillations, respectively (see Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown through clustering analysis of microarray data.

claim: Transcripts for genes in Clusters 2 and 3 accumulate fast or increase slowly and steadily over many cycles of NF-κB oscillations, respectively.
source: The train of p65 nuclear translocations is thus decoded by the cell into different transcriptional dynamics: genes in Cluster 1 display a clear and sustained oscillation in transcript level; instead, transcripts for genes in Clusters 2 and 3 accumulate fast or increase slowly and steadily over many cycles of NF-κB oscillations, respectively (see Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown through clustering analysis of microarray data.

claim: Each new wave of TNF-α elicits on Cluster 1 genes almost the same responses as the previous waves, and no memory is kept of the past.
source: The result is that each new wave of TNF-α elicits on Cluster 1 genes almost the same responses as the previous waves, and no memory is kept of the past; the expression of genes of Clusters 2 and 3 allows a long-lasting response that integrates over time the responses to previous waves.
evidence: This is inferred from the oscillatory pattern of Cluster 1 genes that reset with each stimulus.

claim: The expression of genes of Clusters 2 and 3 allows a long-lasting response that integrates over time the responses to previous waves.
source: The result is that each new wave of TNF-α elicits on Cluster 1 genes almost the same responses as the previous waves, and no memory is kept of the past; the expression of genes of Clusters 2 and 3 allows a long-lasting response that integrates over time the responses to previous waves.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulating pattern of Cluster 2 and 3 genes.

claim: All three dynamics of genes with increased expression could be reproduced by the minimal mathematical model of transcription.
source: All three dynamics of genes with increased expression could be reproduced by our minimal mathematical model of transcription, which incorporates the features of the paradigmatic telegraph model (Suter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated through model fitting to experimental data.

claim: mRNA degradation is the key parameter that allows a functional and temporal shaping of the NF-κB response, in particular for transcripts in Cluster 1.
source: Our model also suggests that mRNA degradation is the key parameter that allows a functional and temporal shaping of the NF-κB response, in particular for transcripts in Cluster 1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 6, top-left panel).
evidence: This is determined through parameter analysis of model fits.

claim: Zfp36 is in Cluster 1 and oscillates sharply and synchronously with the forcing.
source: Of note, Zfp36 is in Cluster 1, and oscillates sharply and synchronously with the forcing; this might contribute further to the shaping of peaked responses.
evidence: This is observed in the microarray data and clustering results.

claim: NF-κB oscillations drive the expression of distinct sets of genes whose expression dynamics and functions correlate.
source: Overall, our most remarkable finding is that NF-κB oscillations drive the expression of distinct sets of genes whose expression dynamics and functions correlate: the transcripts that oscillate encode mostly cytokines and cytokine receptors, the ones that rise fast and decrease slowly encode proteins involved in immunity, and the ones that rise steadily encode proteins involved in the rearrangement of the extracellular matrix (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through clustering and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The transcripts that oscillate encode mostly cytokines and cytokine receptors.
source: Overall, our most remarkable finding is that NF-κB oscillations drive the expression of distinct sets of genes whose expression dynamics and functions correlate: the transcripts that oscillate encode mostly cytokines and cytokine receptors, the ones that rise fast and decrease slowly encode proteins involved in immunity, and the ones that rise steadily encode proteins involved in the rearrangement of the extracellular matrix (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown through pathway enrichment analysis of Cluster 1.

claim: Transcripts that rise fast and decrease slowly encode proteins involved in immunity.
source: Overall, our most remarkable finding is that NF-κB oscillations drive the expression of distinct sets of genes whose expression dynamics and functions correlate: the transcripts that oscillate encode mostly cytokines and cytokine receptors, the ones that rise fast and decrease slowly encode proteins involved in immunity, and the ones that rise steadily encode proteins involved in the rearrangement of the extracellular matrix (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown through pathway enrichment analysis of Cluster 2.

claim: Transcripts that rise steadily encode proteins involved in the rearrangement of the extracellular matrix.
source: Overall, our most remarkable finding is that NF-κB oscillations drive the expression of distinct sets of genes whose expression dynamics and functions correlate: the transcripts that oscillate encode mostly cytokines and cytokine receptors, the ones that rise fast and decrease slowly encode proteins involved in immunity, and the ones that rise steadily encode proteins involved in the rearrangement of the extracellular matrix (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown through pathway enrichment analysis of Cluster 3.

claim: Oscillating transcription programs can be best achieved with oscillating transcription factors.
source: While steady-rise and rise/decline programs of gene expression can be operated by non-oscillatory transcription factors, oscillating transcription programs can be best achieved with oscillating transcription factors.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between TF dynamics and gene expression patterns.

claim: The oscillatory dynamics of NF-κB allows time to be segmented in units of 90 min cycles, with the option to resume chemokine-directed migration after each single cycle.
source: The oscillatory dynamics of NF-κB allows time to be segmented in units of 90 min cycles, with the option to resume chemokine-directed migration after each single cycle.
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation of the oscillatory dynamics.

claim: In the presence of constant stimulation each motile cell will decide for itself, without synchrony to nearby cells.
source: As seen from this perspective, the operation of the NF-κB system as a damped, fast-detuning oscillator implies that in the presence of constant stimulation each motile cell will decide for itself, without synchrony to nearby cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the damped oscillator behavior and lack of synchrony under constant stimulation.

claim: In a situation where stimuli change over time beyond a certain threshold, cells would be broadly coordinated.
source: In contrast, in a situation where stimuli change over time beyond a certain threshold – at least three-fold variation in amplitude – cells would be broadly coordinated.
evidence: This is inferred from the synchronization observed under periodic forcing with sufficient amplitude.

claim: Uncoordinated movement may maximize the volume randomly patrolled by cells.
source: Uncoordinated movement may maximize the volume randomly patrolled by cells, while coordinated movement may be optimal to reach a specific target location.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional consequences of synchronized vs. unsynchronized dynamics.

claim: Coordinated movement may be optimal to reach a specific target location.
source: Uncoordinated movement may maximize the volume randomly patrolled by cells, while coordinated movement may be optimal to reach a specific target location.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional consequences of synchronized dynamics.

claim: The oscillatory dynamics of NF-κB is a means of segmenting time to provide opportunity windows for decision.
source: In conclusion, we suggest that the oscillatory dynamics of NF-κB (and other transcription factors) is a means of segmenting time to provide opportunity windows for decision.
evidence: This is the main proposed interpretation of the biological significance of NF-κB oscillations.
